claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis kills more humans than any other infection.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) kills more humans than any other infection and is characterised by a spatially organised immune response and extracellular matrix remodelling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a factual assertion about TB mortality.

claim: Tuberculosis is characterised by a spatially organised immune response.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) kills more humans than any other infection and is characterised by a spatially organised immune response and extracellular matrix remodelling.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic feature of TB in the abstract.

claim: Tuberculosis is characterised by extracellular matrix remodelling.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) kills more humans than any other infection and is characterised by a spatially organised immune response and extracellular matrix remodelling.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic feature of TB in the abstract.

claim: Infection in 3-D led to greater cellular survival compared to 2-D culture.
source: Infection in 3-D led to greater cellular survival and permitted longitudinal analysis over 21 days.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: 3-D culture permitted longitudinal analysis over 21 days.
source: Infection in 3-D led to greater cellular survival and permitted longitudinal analysis over 21 days.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a capability of the 3-D system.

claim: Key features of human tuberculosis develop in the 3-D model.
source: Key features of human tuberculosis develop, and extracellular matrix integrity favours the host over the pathogen.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: Extracellular matrix integrity favours the host over the pathogen.
source: Key features of human tuberculosis develop, and extracellular matrix integrity favours the host over the pathogen.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: Cell biology differs between traditional cell culture and 3-dimensional systems.
source: An emerging paradigm in biology is that events in traditional 2-dimensional cell culture often differ from those in 3-dimensional (3-D) culture (Benam et al., 2015; Pampaloni et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The extracellular matrix regulates cell biology.
source: Furthermore, the extracellular matrix regulates cell biology (Yamada and Cukierman, 2007; Schwartz and Chen, 2013; Parker et al., 2014) and infection biology differs between 2-D and 3-D systems (Cheng et al., 2011; Barrila et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Infection biology differs between 2-D and 3-D systems.
source: Furthermore, the extracellular matrix regulates cell biology (Yamada and Cukierman, 2007; Schwartz and Chen, 2013; Parker et al., 2014) and infection biology differs between 2-D and 3-D systems (Cheng et al., 2011; Barrila et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis continues to kill 1.5 million people per year.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is a pathogen of global significance that continues to kill 1.5 million people per year (O'Garra et al., 2013; Horsburgh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Recent clinical trials to reduce the global burden of tuberculosis have been unsuccessful.
source: Unfortunately, despite major investment in research, recent clinical trials and vaccine studies to reduce the global burden of tuberculosis (TB) have been unsuccessful (Tameris et al., 2013; Ndiaye et al., 2015; Warner and Mizrahi, 2014), indicating that the model systems that informed these studies require further refinement.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Recent vaccine studies to reduce the global burden of tuberculosis have been unsuccessful.
source: Unfortunately, despite major investment in research, recent clinical trials and vaccine studies to reduce the global burden of tuberculosis (TB) have been unsuccessful (Tameris et al., 2013; Ndiaye et al., 2015; Warner and Mizrahi, 2014), indicating that the model systems that informed these studies require further refinement.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The immune response is necessary for containment of TB infection.
source: In TB, the host-pathogen interaction is highly complex, with the immune response concurrently necessary for containment of infection but paradoxically also driving immunopathology that leads to lung destruction and transmission (Russell, 2011; Elkington and Friedland, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The immune response drives immunopathology that leads to lung destruction and transmission in TB.
source: In TB, the host-pathogen interaction is highly complex, with the immune response concurrently necessary for containment of infection but paradoxically also driving immunopathology that leads to lung destruction and transmission (Russell, 2011; Elkington and Friedland, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Inflammatory conditions in the mouse differ from man.
source: The mouse is the principal model system to study TB, but inflammatory conditions in the mouse differ from man (Seok et al., 2013), and lung pathology is different in murine Mtb infection (Young, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Lung pathology is different in murine Mtb infection compared to human TB.
source: The mouse is the principal model system to study TB, but inflammatory conditions in the mouse differ from man (Seok et al., 2013), and lung pathology is different in murine Mtb infection (Young, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Mtb is an obligate human pathogen.
source: Mtb is an obligate human pathogen and has a very prolonged interaction with host cells, surviving within professional phagocytes (Russell, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Mtb has a very prolonged interaction with host cells.
source: Mtb is an obligate human pathogen and has a very prolonged interaction with host cells, surviving within professional phagocytes (Russell, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Mtb survives within professional phagocytes.
source: Mtb is an obligate human pathogen and has a very prolonged interaction with host cells, surviving within professional phagocytes (Russell, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Cellular survival is greatly prolonged in 3-D cell culture incorporating extracellular matrix.
source: A specific advantage of 3-D cell culture incorporating extracellular matrix is that cellular survival is greatly prolonged (Buchheit et al., 2012; Mueller-Klieser, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Inflammatory signalling in TB granulomas is spatially organised.
source: Furthermore, inflammatory signalling in TB granulomas is spatially organised (Marakalala et al., 2016), with specific microenvironments (Mattila et al., 2013), and the extracellular matrix regulates cell survival in TB (Al Shammari et al., 2015), indicating that an optimal system to study human disease will need to be 3-D with extracellular matrix.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: TB granulomas have specific microenvironments.
source: Furthermore, inflammatory signalling in TB granulomas is spatially organised (Marakalala et al., 2016), with specific microenvironments (Mattila et al., 2013), and the extracellular matrix regulates cell survival in TB (Al Shammari et al., 2015), indicating that an optimal system to study human disease will need to be 3-D with extracellular matrix.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The extracellular matrix regulates cell survival in TB.
source: Furthermore, inflammatory signalling in TB granulomas is spatially organised (Marakalala et al., 2016), with specific microenvironments (Mattila et al., 2013), and the extracellular matrix regulates cell survival in TB (Al Shammari et al., 2015), indicating that an optimal system to study human disease will need to be 3-D with extracellular matrix.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Cells are evenly distributed within microspheres immediately after generation.
source: Immediately after generation, cells are evenly distributed within microspheres and by day seven cellular aggregates start to form (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 1A and B.

claim: By day seven cellular aggregates start to form in microspheres.
source: Immediately after generation, cells are evenly distributed within microspheres and by day seven cellular aggregates start to form (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 1A and B.

claim: There are significantly more aggregates in infected microspheres than uninfected microspheres.
source: Quantitation demonstrated significantly more aggregates in infected microspheres than unifected microspheres (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: One day after infection, a quarter of monocytes had phagocytosed Mtb.
source: One day after infection, a quarter of monocytes had phagocytosed Mtb, analyzed by flow cytometric analysis of cells infected with GFP-expressing Mtb (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 1D.

claim: After 14 days of incubation, large cellular aggregates are observed.
source: After 14 days of incubation, large cellular aggregates are observed (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 1E.

claim: Survival of Mtb-infected cells in 3-D collagen-alginate microspheres was much greater than in 2-D culture.
source: Survival of Mtb-infected cells in 3-D collagen-alginate microspheres was much greater than in 2-D culture, as analyzed by LDH release (Figure 1F) and cellular cytotoxicity assays (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: Decapsulation did not significantly affect cell viability, with over 90% cell viability after decapsulation.
source: Decapsulation did not significantly affect cell viability, with over 90% cell viability after decapsulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Monocytes mature into macrophages in infected microspheres, with greater expression of CD68.
source: Monocytes mature into macrophages in infected microspheres, with greater expression of CD68 (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 1H.

claim: Multinucleate giant cells typical of human TB develop within the aggregates.
source: Within the aggregates, multinucleate giant cells typical of human TB develop, stained for CD68 by immunohistochemistry (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 1I.

claim: The multinucleate giant cells in the model are similar to those that occur in human patients with pulmonary TB.
source: These multinucleate giant cells are similar to those that occur in human patients with pulmonary TB (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 1J showing human tissue.

claim: T cell differentiation occurs within microspheres, with a progressive increase in the proportion of CD4+ T cells.
source: T cell differentiation occurs within microspheres, with a progressive increase in the proportion of CD4+ T cells, while the percentage of CD8+ T cells declines (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The percentage of CD8+ T cells declines in microspheres over time.
source: T cell differentiation occurs within microspheres, with a progressive increase in the proportion of CD4+ T cells, while the percentage of CD8+ T cells declines (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: T cell proliferation does not differ between Mtb-infected and uninfected microspheres.
source: T cell proliferation does not differ between Mtb-infected and uninfected microspheres.
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: Mtb proliferates slowly in microspheres with no cells.
source: Mtb in microspheres without human cells grows relatively slowly, whereas in the presence of PBMCs Mtb proliferates over 24 days, reaching the same luminescence as growth in Middlebrook 7H9 broth (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: In the presence of PBMCs Mtb proliferates over 24 days, reaching the same luminescence as growth in Middlebrook 7H9 broth.
source: Mtb in microspheres without human cells grows relatively slowly, whereas in the presence of PBMCs Mtb proliferates over 24 days, reaching the same luminescence as growth in Middlebrook 7H9 broth (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: MMP-1 gene expression is increased within spheres 4 days post infection.
source: Proteases implicated in TB pathogenesis are upregulated, with MMP-1 gene expression increased within spheres 4 days post infection (Figure 2B) and MMP-9 accumulation in media surrounding the spheres peaking at day 7 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: MMP-9 accumulation in media surrounding the spheres peaks at day 7.
source: Proteases implicated in TB pathogenesis are upregulated, with MMP-1 gene expression increased within spheres 4 days post infection (Figure 2B) and MMP-9 accumulation in media surrounding the spheres peaking at day 7 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: Protease activity causes increased degradation of fluorescently labelled collagen within microspheres.
source: This protease activity has a functional effect, causing increased degradation of fluorescently labelled collagen within microspheres (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 2D.

claim: Mtb infection upregulated gene expression of IFN-γ.
source: Mtb infection also upregulated gene expression of IFN-γ (Figure 2E) and drives secretion of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-1β, IL-12, GM-CSF, IP-10 and MCP-1 analyzed by Luminex multiplex array (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that similar cytokines upregulated in human disease are expressed within the microspheres.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 2E.

claim: Mtb infection drives secretion of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-1β, IL-12, GM-CSF, IP-10 and MCP-1.
source: Mtb infection also upregulated gene expression of IFN-γ (Figure 2E) and drives secretion of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-1β, IL-12, GM-CSF, IP-10 and MCP-1 analyzed by Luminex multiplex array (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that similar cytokines upregulated in human disease are expressed within the microspheres.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Similar cytokines upregulated in human disease are expressed within the microspheres.
source: Mtb infection also upregulated gene expression of IFN-γ (Figure 2E) and drives secretion of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-1β, IL-12, GM-CSF, IP-10 and MCP-1 analyzed by Luminex multiplex array (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that similar cytokines upregulated in human disease are expressed within the microspheres.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the cytokine data.

claim: Incorporation of type I collagen significantly reduced cell death after Mtb infection.
source: Incorporation of type I collagen significantly reduced cell death after Mtb infection, while adherence to elastin increased cell death (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: Adherence to elastin increased cell death after Mtb infection.
source: Incorporation of type I collagen significantly reduced cell death after Mtb infection, while adherence to elastin increased cell death (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: PBMCs in collagen-containing microspheres had a significantly greater ability to control Mtb proliferation.
source: PBMCs in collagen-containing microspheres had a significantly greater ability to control Mtb proliferation, with a lower Mtb proliferation from day seven in the presence of collagen (Figure 3C), further demonstrating that matrix integrity regulates the host-pathogen interaction.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 3C.

claim: Apoptosis was increased in collagen-containing spheres compared to spheres with no collagen.
source: Apoptosis, which is considered a host protective mechanism, was increased in collagen-containing spheres compared to spheres with no collagen (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 3D.

claim: The NADP-NADPH ratio was higher in collagen-containing spheres.
source: In addition, the NADP-NADPH ratio was higher in collagen-containing spheres (Figure 3E), demonstrating divergent cellular energy homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 3E.

claim: Secretion of multiple proinflammatory cytokines in microspheres was increased in the presence of collagen, including IL-1β, TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-6, IL-8 and MCP-1.
source: Secretion of multiple proinflammatory cytokines in microspheres was increased in the presence of collagen, including IL-1β, TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-6, IL-8 and MCP-1 (Figure 3F–K).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figures 3F-K.

claim: Addition of exogenous IFN-β resulted in a minor but significant suppression of Mtb growth.
source: Addition of exogenous IFN-β resulted in a minor but significant suppression of Mtb growth (Figure 4A), whereas in contrast addition of IFN-γ consistently increased growth (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 4A.

claim: Addition of IFN-γ consistently increased Mtb growth.
source: Addition of exogenous IFN-β resulted in a minor but significant suppression of Mtb growth (Figure 4A), whereas in contrast addition of IFN-γ consistently increased growth (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 4B.

claim: Both IFN-β and IFN-γ reduced cellular toxicity in Mtb-infected microspheres.
source: Both IFN-β and IFN-γ reduced cellular toxicity in Mtb-infected microspheres (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figures 4C and D.

claim: IFN-β suppressed MMP-1 mRNA expression while IFN-γ increased MMP-1 expression.
source: However, collagenase activity was divergently regulated, as IFN-β suppressed MMP-1 mRNA expression while IFN-γ increased MMP-1 expression (Figure 4E), suggesting that IFN-β has a matrix-protective role.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 4E.

claim: IFN-β has a matrix-protective role.
source: However, collagenase activity was divergently regulated, as IFN-β suppressed MMP-1 mRNA expression while IFN-γ increased MMP-1 expression (Figure 4E), suggesting that IFN-β has a matrix-protective role.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the MMP-1 data.

claim: Mtb infection increased IFN-γ secretion, and this was further increased by IFN-β.
source: Mtb infection increased IFN-γ secretion, and this was further increased by IFN-β (Figure 4I), demonstrating complex cross-talk between these two cytokines.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 4I.

claim: Augmentation with exogenous PGE2 suppressed Mtb growth in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Augmentation with exogenous PGE2 suppressed Mtb growth in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5A), consistent with findings in the mouse model of Mtb (Mayer-Barber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 5A.

claim: The reduced Mtb luminescence with PGE2 treatment correlated with colony counts when microspheres were lysed and plated on Middlebrook 7H11 agar at day 22.
source: The reduced Mtb luminescence correlated with colony counts when microspheres were lysed and plated on Middlebrook 7H11 agar at day 22 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 5B.

claim: PGE2 increased secretion of proinflammatory IL-6 and IL-8.
source: However, this improved control of bacterial growth was not without potential harmful effects. Secretion of proinflammatory IL-6 and IL-8, a potent neutrophil chemoattractant, was increased by PGE2 (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figures 5C and D.

claim: Secretion of IFN-γ was suppressed by high dose PGE2.
source: Conversely, secretion of IFN-γ was suppressed by high dose PGE2 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 5E.

claim: PGE2 increased cell toxicity.
source: In addition, PGE2 increased cell toxicity (Figure 5F) and suppressed total cell viability (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 5F.

claim: PGE2 suppressed total cell viability.
source: In addition, PGE2 increased cell toxicity (Figure 5F) and suppressed total cell viability (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 5G.

claim: PGE2 reduced caspase 3/7 activity, indicating suppression of apoptosis.
source: PGE2 reduced caspase 3/7 activity, indicating suppression of apoptosis (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 5H.

claim: ESAT-6 or CFP-10 specific T cell lines proliferated in the Mtb infected microspheres but not uninfected spheres.
source: ESAT-6 or CFP-10 specific T cell lines, which respond to antigens secreted via the pathogenicity RD1 locus, proliferated in the Mtb infected microspheres but not uninfected spheres (Figure 6B), which was statistically significant from day seven on quantitation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: Immunoaugmentation with either ESAT-6 or CFP-10 T cell lines led to increased Mtb growth within microspheres compared to infected PBMCs alone.
source: Surprisingly, immunoaugmentation with either ESAT-6 or CFP-10 T cell lines led to increased Mtb growth within microspheres compared to infected PBMCs alone (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 6D.

claim: Augmentation with an autologous innate iNKT cell line has no effect on Mtb growth.
source: Augmentation with an autologous innate iNKT cell line has no effect on Mtb growth (Figure 6E), demonstrating that this was not a generic response to T cell supplementation within the microspheres.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 6E.

claim: Immunoaugmentation with ESAT-6 and CFP-10 lines significantly increased secretion of multiple cytokines, including TNF-α and IL-1β into the media around microspheres.
source: Immunoaugmentation with ESAT-6 and CFP-10 lines significantly increased secretion of multiple cytokines, including TNF-α and IL-1β into the media around microspheres (Figure 6F and G and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figures 6F, 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Augmentation did not significantly affect cell toxicity within infected microspheres.
source: In contrast, augmentation did not significantly affect cell toxicity within infected microspheres (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 6H.

claim: The bioengineering approach differs significantly from traditional model systems to investigate TB.
source: Our bioengineering approach differs significantly from traditional model systems to investigate TB, which predominantly rely on culture of human cells in 2D culture systems without extracellular matrix, infection of the zebrafish larvae with M. marinum or infection of mice with Mtb (Young, 2009; Guirado and Schlesinger, 2013; Vogt and Nathan, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Key findings in the mouse have been replicated in man, such as critical roles for CD4+ T cells, TNF-α and IFN-γ.
source: The mouse model of TB has many advantages and key findings in the mouse have been replicated in man, such as critical roles for CD4+ T cells, TNF-α and IFN-γ (Flynn and Chan, 2001), but pathology in the mouse differs from human TB (Young, 2009) and humanised mice are required to generate caseating lesions (Calderon et al., 2013; Heuts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Humanised mice are required to generate caseating lesions in TB models.
source: The mouse model of TB has many advantages and key findings in the mouse have been replicated in man, such as critical roles for CD4+ T cells, TNF-α and IFN-γ (Flynn and Chan, 2001), but pathology in the mouse differs from human TB (Young, 2009) and humanised mice are required to generate caseating lesions (Calderon et al., 2013; Heuts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: A significant role for IFN-β in the host immune response to TB is emerging from genomic studies.
source: For example, a significant role for IFN-β in the host immune response to TB is emerging from genomic studies, though it remains controversial as to whether this is protective or harmful (Cliff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Several previous studies have shown that IFN-γ increases Mtb growth in primary human cells.
source: Consistent with our findings, several previous studies have shown that IFN-γ increases Mtb growth in primary human cells (Vogt and Nathan, 2011; Douvas et al., 1985; Rook et al., 1986; Crowle and Elkins, 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: A high PPD response associates with the subsequent development of TB.
source: However, cohort studies have shown that a high PPD response, or high IFN-γ response to ESAT-6 or CFP-10, associates with the subsequent development of TB (Comstock et al., 1974; Higuchi et al., 2008; del Corral et al., 2009), suggesting that an excessive IFN-γ response may be deleterious.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: A high IFN-γ response to ESAT-6 or CFP-10 associates with the subsequent development of TB.
source: However, cohort studies have shown that a high PPD response, or high IFN-γ response to ESAT-6 or CFP-10, associates with the subsequent development of TB (Comstock et al., 1974; Higuchi et al., 2008; del Corral et al., 2009), suggesting that an excessive IFN-γ response may be deleterious.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Neutrophil recruitment has been described to have a deleterious effect on host control of infection.
source: Neutrophil recruitment has been described to have a deleterious effect on host control of infection (Kimmey et al., 2015; Nouailles et al., 2014) and therefore there is potential that this may favour Mtb, driving increased pathology, lung destruction and transmission.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: T cell epitopes are hyperconserved in pathogenic mycobacteria.
source: Our findings are consistent with the recent observations that T cell epitopes are hyperconserved in pathogenic mycobacteria (Comas et al., 2010; Coscolla et al., 2015; Lindestam Arlehamn et al., 2015), indicating an evolutionary advantage to the pathogen of specifically stimulating components of the host immune response to facilitate transmission (Orme et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: An excessive immune response in patients is associated with greater pulmonary pathology.
source: For example, an excessive immune response in patients is associated with greater pulmonary pathology (Kaufmann and Dorhoi, 2013; Comstock et al., 1974; Philips and Ernst, 2012; Nunes-Alves et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Pathogenic mycobacteria express ESAT-6 and CFP-10.
source: Similarly, our immunoaugmentation studies concur with the expression of ESAT-6 and CFP-10 by pathogenic mycobacteria, implying a critical role in causing disease (Brites and Gagneux, 2015).
evidence: This is implied by the discussion of immunoaugmentation studies and cited reference.

claim: Ultrapure medium viscosity guluronate (MVG)-dominant alginate had optimal biophysical properties for electrospraying and minimal immunogenicity.
source: Characterisation of different alginates indicated that ultrapure medium viscosity guluronate (MVG)-dominant alginate had optimal biophysical properties for electrospraying and minimal immunogenicity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: PBMCs were isolated from healthy donors recruited from a region of very low TB incidence.
source: These healthy donors were all recruited from a region of very low TB incidence.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Microspheres of 600 μm diameter formed in an ionotropic gelling bath of 100 mM CaCl2 in HBSS.
source: Microspheres of 600 μm diameter formed in an ionotropic gelling bath of 100 mM CaCl2 in HBSS placed below the electrostatic ring that accelerated the microspheres from the needle head.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: No media changes were performed during microsphere culture.
source: No media changes were performed, and the supernatant was harvested at defined time points for analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Mtb growth within microspheres was monitored longitudinally by luminescence.
source: Mtb growth within microspheres was monitored longitudinally by luminescence (GloMax 20/20 Luminometer, Promega).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
